idiom_name: parser/rubocop-ast AST::Processor with on_send / on_def hooks
implementation_notes: Ruby has no overloading and no static types, so the visitor becomes a dispatch table: nodes are tagged with a type symbol, and the operation is an object whose handler methods are named after those types (on_send, on_def, ...), selected with send("on_#{node.type}", node). That is what the parser gem's AST::Processor does and what rubocop-ast layers over the wrapper nodes, memoising the method table (TYPE_TO_METHOD) and visiting children from a generated callback per node type; a rule that only cares about a few node kinds overrides just those handlers and lets the generic case walk on. Because dispatch is by name, coverage is a runtime property: an unimplemented node type takes the generic path instead of failing, which is the price of the flexibility.
code_sketch:
class Metrics < Parser::AST::Processor        # one operation per class
  attr_reader :methods
  def initialize; @methods = []; end

  def on_def(node)                             # handler named after node.type
    @methods << node.children[0]
    super                                      # super visits children
  end
end

metrics = Metrics.new.process(ast)             # framework drives the walk
pitfalls: A typo in a handler name is a method that never fires; Ruby will not tell you, so drive dispatch through a base class that raises or counts unhandled types, as rubocop-ast's debug hooks do.
on_* handlers only run if the traverser actually reaches the node, so a custom walk must include the child template for every node type it hopes to cover.
Handler names come from the parser's node-type vocabulary, which changes between parser versions; pinning the parser gem and checking node types during upgrade is part of the job.

rubocop-ast's descendant traversal (each_node, each_descendant) plus node patterns is the more idiomatic way to express simple checks; a full Processor is worth it only when one operation must react to many node kinds.

variants.name: case/in pattern matching over structured nodes
variants.idiom_name: case/in expression matching array, hash or deconstructable nodes
variants.implementation_notes: Since Ruby 3.0 the case/in expression matches deeply into arrays, hashes and objects that respond to deconstruct/deconstruct_keys, and a case without a matching branch (and without else) raises NoMatchingPatternError - the dynamic analogue of an exhaustiveness check, because an unknown node shape fails loudly instead of silently falling through. It replaces the handler-object visitor when operations can live as free functions and the nodes are plain structures; it does not help when node types are classes with their own behaviour, where the on_*-handler form reads better and keeps traversal in one place.
variants.code_sketch:
def evaluate(node)
  case node
  in [:num, value]       then value            # array-shaped node
  in [:add, left, right] then evaluate(left) + evaluate(right)
  end                                            # no else: raises if unmatched
end
pitfalls: Array patterns match the whole array (unlike hash patterns, which tolerate extra keys), so a node that gains an extra child stops matching an otherwise correct arm; use find patterns or match the hash form.
The raise-on-no-match behaviour is a runtime check: an operation compiled against the old node set fails when the first unseen shape arrives, not at load time.
when and in branches cannot be mixed in one case expression, so migrating a dispatcher is all-or-nothing per case.
Deeply nested patterns are powerful but hard to read; extract helpers (or fall back to the operation class) once an arm spans more than a screen.
